extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, graduate TAs, and conference attendees
extracted.subtask_description: Conference-proceedings qualitative studies on mathematics education: one investigating pre-service teachers' example spaces for probability-zero events, and another comparing beliefs and practices of international vs U.S. graduate mathematics teaching assistants using case-study methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicitation task specification (example generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an example of an event with probability zero. Give an example of a more complicated event with probability zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-ended written responses with no time limit, followed by classroom discussion. The prompt is designed to probe participants' personal example spaces and notions of 'more complicated' — consistent with Watson & Mason's 'give another example' instructional strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization scheme for probability-zero examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples were categorised according to how a fraction could be equal to zero: (1) zero divided by a non-zero ('logically impossible'), (2) a non-zero number divided by a constant large number ('estimated to be zero'), (3) a non-zero number divided by a sequence tending to infinity ('probability converging to zero at limit'), and (4) measure-theoretically explainable probability zero (e.g., picking a certain number from an interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts reported (from 60 examples: 50 in category 1, 3 in category 2, 5 in category 3, 2 potentially in category 4). Note: category 4 required measure-theoretic language which participants largely did not reference; classroom discussion suggested overlap between categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of probability generators / source objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse examples by the probability generators used in the random experiment (e.g., dice, coins, marbles, spinner, deck of cards, picking random numbers, real-life objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report frequencies to reveal influence of standard textbook objects: from 60 examples, 32 used dice, 14 used coins, 8 used marbles, 1 spinner, 1 deck of cards, 2 picking random numbers, 2 real life objects — this shows textbook objects' conspicuous impact on example space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of 'more complicated' in participant responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify techniques participants used to make their second example 'more complicated' than the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two main techniques found: combining events (20 of 30 participants) and generalization. Combining subdivides into: impossible-possible combination; impossible-impossible combination (combining two probability-zero events); possible-possible combination with empty intersection (making the intersection logically impossible). Provide example pairs illustrating each type (e.g., rolling a 7 vs rolling a 5 then a 7; infinitely many 1's on die tosses vs two simultaneous infinite-zero events; getting both 3 and 4 on a single die roll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number-treatment and salience in example choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how participants choose particular real numbers when giving examples of picking a number from an interval (e.g., choosing 4.3275 or 1.0000097 rather than small integers or simple fractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: participants avoid 'exposed' or salient numbers (0,1,2,1/3) preferring 'anonymous' numbers; conjectured cause is familiarity from school tasks that emphasise integers/simple fractions. Use as a lens on participants' number sense and what they consider 'safe' examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of measure-theoretic perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider measure theory as a theoretical account to explain probability-zero events (distinguishing countable vs uncountable sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although only two examples could fit this category and participants did not explicitly reference measure concepts, classroom discussion suggested measure-theoretic explanation can subsume or relate to the other three categories; analysts should note absence/presence of measure language when coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant sampling criteria (purposeful / criterion sampling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select participants by purposeful sampling with explicit criteria: membership in the department, nationality classification (international vs U.S. domestic), and whether MTAs taught their own class during the given semester.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the MTA study, 12 MTAs were selected: six international and six U.S. domestic. Use criterion sampling as described by Creswell (2007) to justify case selection for qualitative comparison studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation of data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple data sources for triangulation: observation, questionnaires, and interviews (with digital voice recording).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural order used: observe classes and take condensed/expanded field notes, administer questionnaire (first, to prime participants), then conduct interviews. Triangulation strengthens credibility by corroborating beliefs and practices across instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation procedure and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-participant observation of one class period with condensed field notes followed by expanded field notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe without participation to avoid influencing instruction; use condensed notes during observation and expand them afterward to capture richer detail for later coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview design and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-structured interviews with 12 open-ended questions: six on teaching practices and six on beliefs; interviews audio recorded and transcribed; interviewer takes shorthand notes and uses probes/follow-ups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview length targeted under 45 minutes; questionnaire administered first (<15 minutes). Use probing to elaborate meanings. Ensure recordings are transcribed for coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data analysis: inductive coding and theme identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive analysis to find patterns and salient themes by repeatedly reviewing field notes, transcripts, and questionnaires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative analysis software (NVivo 8 in this study) to organize data, create sections corresponding to interview questions, generate tentative codes, iteratively reduce and combine codes, and re-review the database until stable themes emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic linkage to theoretical framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground analysis in a theoretical framework defining 'beliefs' (e.g., beliefs about mathematics, teaching, student learning, students) and a postpositivist epistemology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literature-derived classifications (Aguirre & Speer; Ernest; Speer; Thompson; Cooney) to interpret findings; acknowledge postpositivist stance that research uncovers approximate truths and patterns rather than absolute verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research question alignment and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame and align methods to answer explicit research questions (e.g., differences in beliefs and teaching practices between international and U.S. MTAs; how pre-service teachers interpret probability-zero events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure task design, sampling, instruments, and analysis procedures explicitly map to the stated research questions so findings address intended aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity caveats regarding beliefs measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that beliefs are difficult to measure precisely and may be inconsistent with observed behaviors; qualitative research aims to discover regular patterns rather than verify absolute truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report findings as patterns and themes; avoid claiming definitive verification. Use triangulation and careful coding to bolster credibility while acknowledging limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical implications and reporting focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame findings to inform practice (e.g., professional development for MTAs, departmental support, instructional strategies for eliciting examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how identified differences or limited example spaces can guide the creation/adaptation of professional development and instructional interventions; articulate actionable recommendations for departments and educators.
